name: Pear (European)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Pear trees grow best in deep, fertile soil that drains well but holds some moisture, a loam or clay-loam is ideal. Pears actually tolerate heavier, wetter ground better than most fruit trees, including some clay, but they still will not stand in water, so avoid a spot where puddles linger. If your soil is very sandy and dries out fast, work in compost and plan to water more, since a thirsty pear drops fruit.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Pear wants a deep, fertile loam to clay-loam with steady moisture and moderate organic matter. It is more forgiving of heavy, moisture-retentive soils than apple or stone fruit, and tolerates a wider pH band, but it still will not accept standing water, which drives crown and root rots. On a wet site, plant on a low berm. One important trade-off: rich soil and heavy nitrogen push the soft, succulent growth that fire blight colonizes, so feed pears lean and favor a fire-blight-tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series) on any site with disease history.

ph.note_beginner: Pear trees like soil that runs from slightly acidic to neutral, a pH around 6.0 to 7.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, where 7.0 is neutral). Pears are a bit more tolerant of alkaline soil than apples. Test your soil before planting, since it is much easier to adjust the pH now than after the tree is in the ground. Garden lime raises a low pH; garden sulfur lowers a high one. Your local extension office can test a sample for you.
ph.note_seasoned: Pear does best at a pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerates roughly 5.5 to 7.5, a slightly wider and more alkaline-tolerant band than apple. Test the soil before planting and adjust the whole root zone, not just the hole, because correcting pH around an established tree is slow. Lime raises a low pH; elemental sulfur lowers a high one. Well outside this band, iron and manganese availability falls and new growth yellows between the veins.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before bud break, guided by shoot growth: a healthy young pear makes about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth a year, so feed to reach that and no more. Excess nitrogen is the classic pear mistake, it drives soft, succulent growth that fire blight runs straight through, and it delays fruiting. Mature trees on fertile soil often need no nitrogen at all. If anything, err on the side of underfeeding a pear.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Feed pear trees once a year, in early spring before the buds open, with a balanced fertilizer, and go light. Too much feeding is the number-one pear mistake: it makes lots of soft new growth that the disease fire blight loves, and it pushes the tree to grow leaves instead of fruit. If the tree is growing well and putting out healthy new branches each year, it may need no feeding at all. When in doubt, use less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced N-P-K ratio (the three numbers on the bag, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) such as 10-10-10 at a modest rate, leaning toward the low end on any vigorous tree to limit fire-blight-prone growth. On fertile ground a pear often wants none.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. A balanced one like 10-10-10 is fine for pears, used sparingly. The first number (nitrogen) is the one to keep low, because too much makes soft growth that catches fire blight.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rule is about 1/8 lb of actual nitrogen per year of tree age, capped near 1/2 to 3/4 lb actual N for a mature tree, noticeably leaner than the apple rule because of fire blight. Always follow the label and skip nitrogen entirely in a year of strong shoot growth.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple guideline is a small amount that grows a little with the tree's age, following the directions on the bag, and using even less than you would for an apple. When in doubt, feed less, an underfed pear is far healthier than an overfed one.

companions.note_beginner: Pears do not pair with other plants the way vegetables do. For a pear, the neighbor that counts is a second, different pear variety that blooms at the same time, within about 50 to 100 ft, because most pears need another pear nearby to make fruit. Right around the trunk, do the opposite of planting companions: keep grass and other plants away from the base out to the edge of the branches, because they steal water and food from the young tree. Use mulch there instead, and never plant a pear near a black walnut tree, which poisons the soil for it.
companions.note_seasoned: Pear does not companion-plant in the vegetable sense; the interactions that matter are pollination and root competition. The single most important neighbor is a second, bloom-overlapping pear variety (the pollinizer) within about 50 to 100 ft, since most pears are self-unfruitful. At the trunk, the rule reverses: keep turf and aggressive perennials out of the root zone, where grass competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen. Maintain a mulched, vegetation-free circle to the dripline, and avoid siting near black walnut, whose juglone is toxic to pear.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: spring bulbs (daffodil)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A ring of daffodils at the drip line is a traditional fruit-tree-guild move with two intended jobs: the early foliage forms a band that helps hold back creeping grass, the tree's main competitor, and daffodils are toxic enough that voles and deer tend to avoid grazing through them to the trunk. They emerge and feed before the canopy leafs out, then go dormant, so they do not compete in summer. Treat this as a useful cultural barrier rather than a measured yield booster.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The daffodil-ring (grass suppression + rodent/deer deterrence via toxicity) is a well-established permaculture fruit-tree-guild practice grounded in daffodils' real toxicity and spring-ephemeral timing, applied to pear the same way it is to apple; not a measured pear yield/health effect. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant a ring of daffodils around your pear tree, out where the branches reach. They come up early in spring, help keep grass from creeping toward the trunk, and because they are poisonous to nibble, they discourage mice and deer. They die back in summer, so they stay out of the tree's way.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: comfrey
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Comfrey is a workhorse of the fruit-tree guild. Its deep taproot pulls from well below the tree's surface feeder roots, so it does not compete for the same water and nutrients, and it shades out grass along the row. Chopped two or three times a season and dropped under the tree, its lush leaves break down into a mineral-rich mulch, and the flowers feed pollinators. The dynamic-accumulator framing is more tradition than proven chemistry, but the practical value as non-competing mulch and grass suppression is real.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Comfrey as chop-and-drop mulch / grass suppressor with a deep non-competing taproot is widely practiced and partly grounded (deep taproot, vigorous biomass); the 'dynamic accumulator' mineral claims are permaculture tradition, not peer-reviewed. Same mechanism whether under apple or pear. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Comfrey is a leafy plant that grows well around fruit trees. Its roots reach deep down, so it does not steal water from the tree, and it crowds out grass. A few times each summer you can cut the big leaves and lay them on the soil under the tree, where they rot down into natural food for it. Its flowers also bring in helpful bees.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: clover (living mulch)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Dutch white clover makes a strong living mulch under pears. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through its root symbiosis, feeding the tree slowly while staying low and tolerating harvest foot traffic. It covers the ground to suppress weeds and hold moisture without the aggressive grass competition bare turf brings. Keep it back from the immediate trunk zone, and note it does draw some moisture, so manage it on dry sites. Because pears want lean nitrogen, treat the clover's slow trickle as a feature, not a reason to also fertilize.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Dutch white clover living mulch = legume N-fixation + weed suppression + walkable cover; mechanistically sound and supported by extension/NRCS orchard legume cover-crop work. mechanistic/medium: real mechanism, held at medium because clover-to-tree N transfer magnitude and net water effect vary by site.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: White clover is a low, soft plant you can grow as a living carpet under your pear tree. It pulls nitrogen from the air and feeds it slowly into the soil, while covering the ground to keep weeds down and hold in moisture. It is tough enough to walk on at picking time. Just keep it from growing right against the trunk.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: black walnut
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Black walnut is a definitive bad neighbor for pear. Its roots, hulls, and leaf litter release juglone, an allelopathic compound toxic to many sensitive plants, and pear (like apple) is among those affected, showing decline and dieback within the walnut's root zone. The effect extends well beyond the visible canopy, roughly to the full root spread (commonly cited at fifty-plus feet from a mature tree), so siting matters more than spacing tweaks: keep pears entirely out of a black walnut's root zone.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Juglone allelopathy is a real, well-characterized chemical mechanism; pome fruit including pear is documented as juglone-sensitive across extension sources. mechanistic/high: the mechanism and pome-fruit sensitivity are well established and uncontested.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep pear trees far away from black walnut trees. Black walnuts release a natural chemical called juglone from their roots and leaves that is poisonous to pears and can make them sicken and die. The chemical spreads through the soil well past the walnut's branches, so give them a very wide berth, at least 50 feet from a big walnut.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: turfgrass to the trunk
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Letting turfgrass grow right up to a pear trunk is a quiet but real drag on the tree, especially when young. Grass competes directly for water and nitrogen in the surface zone where the feeder roots sit, slowing growth and delaying bearing, and dense grass and mulch against the trunk harbor voles that girdle bark over winter. Maintain a vegetation-free or mulched strip about two feet out from the trunk (mulch pulled back a few inches off the bark itself).

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Extension guidance consistently prescribes a vegetation-free/mulched zone around young fruit trees and warns of rodent bark damage from grass/mulch at the trunk; the grass-competition effect on young tree growth is well documented for pome fruit. extension_backed/high.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Do not let lawn grass grow right up against your pear tree's trunk. The grass competes with the young tree for water and food, so it grows slower and fruits later. Grass at the trunk also hides mice that can chew the bark in winter. Keep a clear or mulched circle about two feet around the trunk, with the mulch pulled back slightly so it does not touch the bark.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested pears drop early or are inedible.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic 'worm in the fruit.' You find a small hole with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad pears drop early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the pear. Two or more generations per season in most regions. The same pest attacks apple.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny pears in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad or kaolin clay on a degree-day/petal-fall schedule. Mating disruption works at larger scale.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every pear that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags over young pears to keep moths out, and scent traps help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned pear or apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen pears, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected pear or apple trees make it worse.

pests.name: Pear psylla
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Nymphs feed in clusters on shoots and leaves and exude copious sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; heavy feeding causes leaf scorch, premature drop, fruit russeting, and tree decline. The signature pear pest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves and young pears get coated in a sticky, shiny film that turns black and grimy (sooty mold), and the leaves may scorch and drop. Tiny insects cluster on the new shoots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola; a small psyllid specific to pear that overwinters as an adult and builds several overlapping generations through the season. Outbreaks follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill its natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny pear-specific insect (a kind of jumping plant louse) that sucks sap and oozes sticky stuff. It can build up fast, especially if bug sprays have wiped out the good bugs that normally keep it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant-season horticultural oil to smother overwintering adults and eggs; in-season insecticidal soap or summer oil; conserve natural enemies (anthocorid bugs, lacewings) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides; kaolin clay deters egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil while the tree is dormant in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, and use insecticidal soap in the growing season. Avoid harsh sprays, which kill the helpful bugs that eat psylla.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A well-timed dormant oil program plus a natural-enemy-friendly spray regime is the backbone of psylla management; avoid the lush nitrogen-pushed growth psylla favors.
pests.prevention_beginner: A good dormant oil spray in late winter and going easy on harsh sprays and fertilizer keep this pear-specific pest in check.

pests.name: Pear scab
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves, shoots, and fruit; fruit lesions become corky and cracked, and severe infection causes leaf yellowing and early defoliation. The pear analog of apple scab.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-to-black spots appear on the leaves and the pears get rough, scabby, cracked patches. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; spores overwinter in fallen leaves and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods driven by leaf wetness and temperature. Distinct from the apple-scab fungus but managed the same way.
pests.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives winter in last year's fallen leaves and spreads in cool, wet spring weather onto the new leaves and fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply sulfur or other labeled fungicide on a protective schedule keyed to spring infection periods; far easier to prevent than to cure once established.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring, applied before infection takes hold, is the organic option. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn (destroys the overwintering source), prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
pests.prevention_beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, that is where the fungus hides over winter. Prune for good airflow too.

pests.name: Fabraea leaf spot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous small, dark purple-to-black spots on leaves and fruit through summer; heavy infection causes blotching, early defoliation, and pitted, cracked fruit. Most damaging in warm, humid regions and on susceptible cultivars (Bartlett, Bosc).
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of small dark spots speckle the leaves in mid to late summer, and the tree may drop a lot of leaves early. The pears can get spotted and pitted too.
pests.cause_seasoned: Entomosporium mespili (Fabraea maculata); the fungus overwinters in fallen leaves and infected twigs and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, building late in the season.
pests.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in old fallen leaves and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, getting worse as summer goes on. It is a bigger problem in hot, humid areas.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protective fungicide (labeled product) on a summer schedule where it has a history; rake and destroy fallen leaves to cut the overwintering source.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If your tree gets this every year, a protective fungicide through summer helps. Always rake up and remove the fallen leaves to break the cycle.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Fall leaf removal, airflow pruning, and resistant cultivar choice; the disease is far worse in the humid Southeast than in arid or northern regions.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall, prune so air moves through the tree, and in hot humid areas choose a resistant variety.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic 'shepherd's crook'; affected branches look scorched, and sunken, oozing cankers form on wood. Pear is markedly MORE susceptible than apple, and a single warm, wet bloom can kill whole limbs or a young tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook shape. It can kill whole branches or the whole tree. Pears catch it worse than apples.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through open blossoms and tender shoot tips in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth. It is the single biggest reason European pears fail in the humid South and East.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers and soft new shoots in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse. It is the main reason pears struggle in warm, damp climates.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood at least 8 to 12 inches below visible symptoms, disinfecting tools between cuts, in dry weather; remove badly affected trees. There is no cure once established, management is prevention plus cutting it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage (about a hand's length past it), wiping your pruners with disinfectant between every cut so you do not spread it, and only in dry weather. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The decisive move is variety and rootstock choice: plant fire-blight-resistant cultivars (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Magness) on a tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series). Then avoid excess nitrogen, prune only in dry weather, and follow a bloom-time forecast model where available.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is to choose a resistant variety (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren) on a resistant rootstock, especially where summers are warm and humid. Then go easy on fertilizer (soft growth catches it) and prune only in dry weather.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Olive to black velvety lesions on leaves and fruit that turn corky and cracked; severe infection yellows leaves and causes early defoliation and scabby, misshapen fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy spots on the leaves and rough, scabby, cracked patches on the pears. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; overwinters in fallen leaves and infects during wet spring weather, infection periods set by leaf wetness and temperature.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that overwinters in last year's fallen leaves and spreads onto new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sulfur or a labeled fungicide on a protective spring schedule keyed to infection periods; prevention beats cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring before the spots appear is the organic route. Once it is widespread it is too late for that year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves each autumn, prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall and prune for good airflow. Resistant varieties rarely need spraying.

diseases.name: Fabraea leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Many small dark purple-black spots on leaves and fruit through summer, leading to early defoliation and pitted, cracked fruit; the dominant summer foliar disease of pear in warm, humid regions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Lots of small dark spots cover the leaves in summer, and the tree can drop most of its leaves early. The pears get spotted and pitted.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Entomosporium mespili; overwinters in fallen leaves and twig lesions and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, intensifying late in the season.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in old leaves and twigs and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, getting worse through the summer.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protective fungicide on a summer schedule where it recurs; rigorous fall leaf removal to cut the overwintering inoculum.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A protective fungicide through summer if it keeps coming back, plus raking up all the fallen leaves in fall.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Fall sanitation, airflow pruning, and resistant cultivars; far less of a problem in arid and northern climates.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves, prune for airflow, and pick a resistant variety in hot, humid areas.

diseases.name: Pear decline
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Slow decline, weak growth, small leaves with reddish autumn color, and reduced yield, or in acute cases sudden collapse; driven by a phytoplasma transmitted by pear psylla and expressed through a sensitive rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The tree slowly weakens over years, with small leaves that redden early in fall and a shrinking crop, or sometimes a sudden collapse. It is tied to the pear psylla insect and to certain rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma (a bacteria-like organism) spread by pear psylla; severity depends heavily on rootstock sensitivity, which is why decline-resistant rootstocks (OHxF series) matter.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny disease organism carried by the pear psylla insect. How badly a tree is hit depends on its rootstock, so a resistant rootstock is the main protection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure; manage by controlling pear psylla (the vector) and, at planting, choosing a tolerant rootstock (OHxF). Remove severely declining trees.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a tree has it. Keep pear psylla under control and, most importantly, start with a resistant rootstock when you plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on a decline-tolerant rootstock (OHxF 87/97/333) and keep psylla populations low; avoid highly sensitive rootstocks.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy a tree grown on a resistant rootstock (the OHxF series) and keep pear psylla in check. That is the whole prevention.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep, infrequent irrigation: about 1 inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat and during fruit sizing, tapering off as the tree goes dormant.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not too often, aim for about 1 inch a week while the tree is growing and making fruit. Water more in hot, dry spells and less once the leaves drop in fall.
watering.amount_seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week as a baseline (a deep soak that wets the full root zone), increasing during fruit sizing in mid to late summer; pears drop fruit when droughted at sizing.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch a week. The easiest way is one long, slow soak that gets the water down deep, rather than a quick daily sprinkle.
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or a slow soak at the dripline; keep water off the trunk and crown to avoid collar rot, and mulch to hold moisture (pulled back a few inches from the trunk).
watering.method_beginner: Use a soaker hose or drip line, or let a hose trickle slowly at the edge of the branches. Keep water off the trunk itself, and mulch around the tree (not touching the trunk) to hold moisture in.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, persistently soggy soil, and root or collar rot at the trunk base signal too much water or poor drainage; pear tolerates wet ground better than most fruit trees but not standing water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the leaves yellow and the ground stays soggy, the tree is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Rot at the base of the trunk is a warning sign.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting or scorched leaf margins and premature fruit drop in summer indicate drought stress, especially during fruit sizing.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting or dry, brown leaf edges, and small fruit that drops early, mean the tree is too dry, especially in mid to late summer when the pears are filling out.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Establishment: deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week through the first summer to drive root growth; do not let the root ball dry out.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: First-year tree: give it a deep soak once or twice a week all summer so the roots get established. Do not let it dry out.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Fruit sizing: water weekly and consistently as pears bulk up; steady moisture now prevents premature drop and cracking.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the pears are growing bigger, water once a week and keep it steady, this is when uneven watering makes fruit drop.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Dormant: minimal irrigation; rely on natural precipitation unless soils are unusually dry over a mild winter.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter, when the tree is bare and resting, you barely need to water at all, rain usually covers it.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Consistent soil moisture during fruit sizing prevents premature drop and cracking; a young tree in its establishment year needs the most attention to even watering.
watering.method_note_beginner: Steady, even watering matters most in the first year and while the pears are growing. Big swings between bone-dry and soaked make fruit drop.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Establishment year (root development) and fruit sizing (mid to late summer) are the critical irrigation windows; dormant-season water needs are minimal.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Two times matter most for watering: the first year after planting, and mid-to-late summer when the pears are filling out. In winter the tree needs almost no water.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Not applicable. Pear is planted as a bare-root dormant tree or a potted nursery tree, not started from seed indoors, so there is no tender seedling to harden off. Plant during dormancy (late winter to early spring) and the tree breaks bud already acclimated to outdoor conditions.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: This step does not apply to pears. Hardening off means slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors, but you do not start a pear from seed. You buy a young tree, either bare-root (no soil on the roots) or in a pot, and plant it straight into the ground, so there is nothing to harden off.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a bare-root tree while fully dormant, late winter to early spring, as soon as the ground is workable. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two before planting, dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending, and set the tree so the graft union (the swollen knob where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 in above the final soil line, burying it lets the variety root over and defeats the rootstock. Backfill with native soil, water in to settle, and stake dwarf and quince stocks. A potted tree follows the same depth rule but can go in through spring.
start_method.notes_beginner: If your tree comes bare-root (bare roots, no pot), plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless and dormant, as soon as you can dig the soil. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough that the roots spread out without folding. The key thing: find the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the top variety was joined to the roots) and keep it about 2 to 3 in above the soil, never bury it. Fill the hole with the same soil you dug out, water well, and tie small trees to a stake. A potted tree is planted the same way and can go in anytime through spring.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Fill the pot with bagged potting mix from a garden center, not soil dug from your yard. Garden soil packs down hard in a pot and holds too much water, which rots the roots. Potting mix stays loose and drains well.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost (about a quarter of the pot) to feed the tree, plus a few handfuls of perlite (the little white pellets) or bark to help water drain through. Do not add water-holding crystals, a potted pear is more likely to be harmed by soggy roots than by dry ones.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a high-quality bagged potting mix (a soilless peat- or coir-based medium), not native garden soil or topsoil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container. The mix must be free-draining and stay open over several seasons in the same pot.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in roughly 20 to 30 percent compost for nutrition and moisture buffering, and a handful of coarse material such as perlite or fine bark to keep drainage open. Avoid water-holding gels; a potted pear is far more often lost to wet roots than to drought.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A tree in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground, so check it every day when it is warm. Stick a finger an inch into the mix; if it feels dry, water until it runs out the holes in the bottom. Empty the saucer so the pot is not sitting in water. The goal is moist mix, never dust-dry and never swampy.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Because you water a pot so often, the water washes the food out of the soil, so a potted pear needs feeding a bit more than one in the ground, but still go light because of fire blight. Add a slow-release fertilizer in early spring, and stop feeding by midsummer so the tree is not pushing soft new shoots when cold weather arrives.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Winter is the hard part for a potted pear. In a pot, the roots sit above ground and get cold from every side, so they freeze much more easily than roots in the ground. After the leaves drop and the tree is dormant (resting for winter), move the pot somewhere cold but protected, like an unheated garage or shed, or up against the north side of the house. It still needs the cold to rest, but the shelter keeps the roots from freezing solid. Give it a little water now and then so the soil never dries out completely.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: A potted pear is the winter-vulnerable case: roots in an above-ground pot are exposed to cold from all sides and run several zones less hardy than the same tree in the ground. Once dormant, move the pot to an unheated but sheltered spot (an unheated garage, shed, or against a north wall) where it stays cold enough to hold dormancy but is buffered from the deep-freeze and freeze-thaw swings that kill container roots. Water occasionally so the rootball never fully dries.

container_notes.notes_beginner: Only the smallest pear trees do well in pots, the ones grown on a dwarfing quince or OHxF 333 rootstock (ask the nursery). A normal-size pear tree quickly gets too big for any pot. Every 2 to 3 years, trim some roots and replace the top few inches of mix. And remember the pollination rule still applies: even a potted pear needs a second, different pear variety blooming nearby to make fruit.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers suit pear only on a genuinely size-controlling rootstock (a quince stock, or OHxF 333); a semi-vigorous or standard tree will outgrow any practical pot. Expect to root-prune and refresh the top few inches of mix every 2 to 3 years to keep the tree productive, and remember a potted tree still needs a bloom-overlapping pollinizer nearby. Containers are the realistic route to pears on a patio without space for two full trees, paired with a second potted variety.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Container roots dry out far faster than ground roots, so check moisture daily in warm weather; a 20-gallon pot in summer sun can need water every day or two. Water until it runs from the drainage holes, then let the top inch begin to dry before the next watering. Never let the pot go bone-dry (it drops fruit) and never leave it standing in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so a container pear needs feeding somewhat more often than one in the ground, but keep nitrogen modest because of fire blight. Use a balanced slow-release fertilizer at the start of the season and stop by midsummer so the tree hardens off and does not push tender growth into fall.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering (sub-irrigated) containers are not the first choice for pear. They keep the lower rootball continuously moist, and while pear tolerates damp ground better than apple, a permanently wet pot still risks crown rot. Use a free-draining pot with open drainage holes and water from the top.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots (the kind with a water reservoir in the bottom) for pears. They keep the lower roots wet all the time, which can rot the crown. Use a regular pot with holes in the bottom and water it from the top.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Plan winter protection in from the start in cold zones: a pear hardy to zone 4 in the ground may only survive zone 6 or 7 winters in an exposed pot, because the root zone has no insulating soil mass. In order of protection, sink the pot to its rim in the ground for winter, cluster and wrap pots, or move to an unheated sheltered structure. Do not bring a dormant pear into a heated room, warmth breaks dormancy and the tree misses its winter chill.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: If you live where winters are cold, plan for winter before you even plant. A potted pear is much less cold-hardy than the same tree in the ground, because the roots have no surrounding soil to keep them warm. To protect them, sink the whole pot into a hole in the ground for winter, group pots together and wrap them, or move the pot into an unheated garage or shed. Do not bring the tree indoors where it is warm, the warmth wakes it up too early and it misses the cold it needs to fruit.

recommended.name: Hood
recommended.recommended_note: The lowest-chill pick here (about 200 hours) and the key to fruiting in mild-winter zones; fire-blight resistant. Pair with another low-chill, overlapping-bloom pear such as Kieffer.

recommended.name: Kieffer
recommended.recommended_note: The bulletproof Southern pear: highly fire-blight resistant, heat-tolerant, partially self-fruitful, best for cooking and canning rather than fresh dessert quality.

recommended.name: Orient
recommended.recommended_note: Fire-blight resistant and productive in the South; large, firm fruit good fresh or canned.

recommended.name: Seckel
recommended.recommended_note: Small, intensely sweet 'sugar pear,' somewhat fire-blight resistant. Note: NOT compatible with Bartlett as a pollen partner, pair it with Bosc, Comice, or Moonglow.

recommended.name: Moonglow
recommended.recommended_note: USDA-bred, strongly fire-blight resistant, soft and mild; a reliable pollinizer and a good main crop for humid regions.

recommended.name: Ayers
recommended.recommended_note: Sweet, low-grit dessert pear with good fire-blight resistance; a strong choice for the Southeast.

recommended.name: Warren
recommended.recommended_note: Buttery, high-quality dessert pear, fire-blight resistant and notably cold-hardy; stores well.

recommended.name: Bartlett
recommended.use: fresh eating, canning (the classic; partially self-fruitful)
recommended.recommended_note: The familiar summer pear, partially self-fruitful but heavier with a pollinizer. Fire-blight SUSCEPTIBLE, so best in drier or cooler climates. Will not pollinate Seckel.

recommended.name: Comice
recommended.recommended_note: Doyenne du Comice, the classic gift-box dessert pear, exceptionally rich and buttery; a good partner for Bartlett or Seckel.

recommended.name: Bosc
recommended.recommended_note: Cinnamon-russeted, firm and aromatic, holds shape in baking and stores for months. Fire-blight susceptible. Incompatible with quince rootstock without an interstem.

recommended.name: Anjou
recommended.recommended_note: D'Anjou, the long-storage winter pear, partially self-fruitful and one of the best keepers; needs the longest post-harvest chilling before it will ripen.

recommended.name: Magness
recommended.recommended_note: High-quality, fire-blight resistant dessert pear, but its pollen is STERILE: it cannot pollinate other trees and itself needs TWO other compatible varieties nearby to set fruit.

varieties.note_seasoned: Twelve cultivars sequenced very early to very late by bloom so you can pair overlapping bloom groups for cross-pollination. Chill spans about 200 hours (low-chill Hood) to 800 (Bartlett); match it to your winters. For the humid Southeast, lean on the fire-blight-resistant set (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Magness); Bartlett, Bosc, and Comice are dessert-quality but blight-susceptible and want drier or cooler air. Mind two pairing rules: Bartlett and Seckel will not cross, and Magness is pollen-sterile (needs two partners).
varieties.note_beginner: Pick at least two different varieties that bloom around the same time so they can pollinate each other. Where summers are warm and humid, choose fire-blight-resistant kinds like Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, or Warren. In drier or cooler areas you can grow the famous dessert pears (Bartlett, Bosc, Comice). Two gotchas: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, and Magness cannot pollinate anything, so do not rely on it as a partner.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Once ripened, pears hold only a few days at room temperature; ripen them in small batches as needed. Unripened, firm summer pears (Bartlett) ripen in 4 to 7 days at room temperature, winter pears need a cold period first.
storage.room_temp_beginner: A ripe pear stays good only a few days on the counter, so ripen just a few at a time. A firm, unripe summer pear like Bartlett takes about 4 to 7 days to soften at room temperature.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Held firm and unripe near 30 to 35°F at high humidity, summer pears (Bartlett) keep 2 to 3 months and winter pears (Anjou, Bosc, Comice) keep 3 to 5 months. The cold also satisfies the post-harvest chilling many varieties need before they will ripen at room temperature. Pull a few out to ripen as wanted.
storage.fridge_beginner: In the fridge, firm unripe pears last a long time, about 2 to 3 months for summer Bartlett and up to 4 to 5 months for winter pears like Anjou and Bosc. The cold storage also does double duty: many pears need that chill before they will ripen properly on the counter. Take out a few at a time to ripen.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Pears do not freeze well whole (texture turns mushy); freeze as slices in light syrup or as sauce for cooking use up to about a year.
storage.freezer_beginner: Whole pears turn mushy if frozen. Instead, peel and slice them into a little light syrup, or cook them down first, then freeze. Frozen this way they keep about a year and are great for baking.
storage.notes_seasoned: The pear rule that trips everyone up: pick MATURE BUT FIRM and ripen off the tree. Most varieties need a cold rest first (a few days for summer pears, several weeks near freezing for winter pears like Anjou), then ripen at room temperature until the neck yields. A pear ripened on the tree, or held too warm too long, breaks down brown and gritty at the core. Handle gently, bruised fruit rots fast.
storage.notes_beginner: Here is the pear secret: pick them while still firm and green, then ripen them indoors, never on the tree. Most kinds need a stretch in the fridge first (a few days for summer pears, a few weeks for winter ones), then they finish ripening on the counter until the stem end softens. A pear left to ripen on the tree turns brown and gritty inside. Handle them gently so they do not bruise.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Not applicable as annual rotation: pear is a permanent tree that holds its site for decades. The real concern is replant disease, avoid planting a new pear where an old pear or apple stood, or replace the soil in the planting hole and choose a vigorous rootstock.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Crop rotation is for annual vegetables, not pear trees, a pear stays in one spot for many years. The one thing to know: do not plant a new pear exactly where an old pear (or apple) used to be, because leftover soil problems can stunt the new tree. Pick a fresh spot, or dig out and replace the old soil.
rotation.note_seasoned: Site selection, not rotation, is the lever: full sun, well-drained soil (pear tolerates heavier ground than most fruit), good air movement to limit fire blight and Fabraea, and fresh ground free of replant issues.
rotation.note_beginner: Instead of rotating, just choose a good permanent spot: full sun, soil that drains (pears handle heavier soil than most fruit trees), and open air around the tree to keep disease down.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root, dormant)
growth_stages.timing: late winter to early spring, while dormant
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant, leafless bare-root or potted young tree with a visible graft union; buds tight and not yet swelling. Roots should be moist and pliable, not dried out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: You are planting a small, leafless tree, often sold bare-root (no pot, roots wrapped). Look for a bump low on the trunk, that is the graft where your pear variety joins the rootstock, and keep it above the soil line.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant while dormant in well-drained full sun; keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the soil line; water in deeply; stake if on a dwarfing or quince rootstock. Do not fertilize at planting.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant it in early spring in a sunny, well-drained spot, before the buds open. Keep that graft bump above the ground, water it in well, and stake it if it is a small tree. Hold off on fertilizer for now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record planting date, variety, rootstock, and pollinizer planted nearby.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the date you planted, which pear variety, and which second variety you planted nearby to pollinate it.

growth_stages.name: Year-1 establishment (remove blossoms)
growth_stages.timing: first spring and summer after planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves and shoots emerge; the tree may attempt to flower. Watch for steady new shoot growth (the sign roots are taking) and for any blackened shoot tips (early fire blight).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The tree leafs out and grows its first new shoots. It may even try to flower, do not let it. Watch for any branch tips that suddenly turn black and bend over.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove any blossoms that open this first year so energy goes to roots and scaffold. Keep soil evenly moist (deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week), mulch, protect the trunk from rodents and sunscald, and prune only lightly and only in dry weather to limit fire blight.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If flowers open this first year, pinch them off, the tree is too young to fruit. Water deeply once or twice a week, mulch (not touching the trunk), and let it build roots. No pears this year is exactly right.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note first-year shoot growth, whether blossoms were removed, and any fire-blight strikes cut out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Jot down how much the tree grew and that you removed the first flowers.

growth_stages.name: Scaffold formation (years 1 to 4)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The permanent branch framework develops. Pears grow naturally upright and narrow, so look for well-spaced scaffolds and work to widen their crotch angles with spreaders.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Over the first few years the tree builds its main branches. Pears want to grow tall and narrow, so you want to encourage a few strong branches that spread outward.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Each winter, prune lightly in dry weather to train structure: keep a central leader, select well-spaced scaffolds, and use limb spreaders to widen the naturally narrow crotch angles. Prune conservatively, heavy cuts force the succulent regrowth fire blight exploits.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each winter while the tree is bare and the weather is dry, do some light shaping: keep one main upright stem and a few evenly spaced side branches, and gently spread upright branches outward with small spacers. Go easy, hard pruning makes soft growth that catches disease.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record dormant-pruning date, branches removed, and spreaders placed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you pruned and what you shaped.

growth_stages.name: Annual winter dormant prune
growth_stages.timing: late winter (about February to March), before bud break, in dry weather
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless, dormant canopy, the time to shape structure. Note water sprouts, crossing limbs, and any blackened fire-blight wood or cankers to remove.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In late winter the tree is bare, the best time to prune because you can see the branches. Look for any black, scorched-looking wood from fire blight.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune annually in late winter, in dry weather: thin for light and air, remove water sprouts, crossing, and dead wood, and cut out fire-blight cankers 8 to 12 inches below the damage, disinfecting tools between cuts. Keep cuts moderate.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Once a year, in late winter and only when it is dry out, thin the branches so sunlight and air get in, and remove dead or crossing wood. If you see any fire-blight-burned branch, cut well below it and wipe your tools with disinfectant between cuts.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record annual prune date and any disease wood removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the date you pruned and anything diseased you took out.

growth_stages.name: Bloom and pollination
growth_stages.timing: early spring, after chill is satisfied (often just before apples)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds open to white blossoms, generally a few days before apples. Watch for bee activity (pear nectar is low, so bees can be sparse) and check that a compatible pollinizer is blooming at the same time. Warm, wet bloom weather is the fire-blight danger window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The tree covers itself in white flowers, a bit earlier than apples. Bees should be visiting. Check that your second pear variety is flowering too, and watch the weather, warm and wet during bloom is when fire blight spreads.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not apply insecticide during bloom (it kills pollinators). Watch the frost forecast and protect open bloom from late frost. Ensure a compatible pollinizer is in bloom within about 50 to 100 ft. In warm, wet weather, follow a fire-blight forecast and avoid pruning.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Never spray bug killer while the tree is in bloom, you would kill the bees you need. Cover small trees if a hard frost is coming, since frost on open flowers means no pears. Make sure your second pear variety is blooming too, and do not prune in warm, wet weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record bloom start, overlap with pollinizer, frost events, and bloom-time weather.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when blooming started, whether your two trees overlapped, and any frosts.

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and thinning
growth_stages.timing: late spring to early summer, after petal fall
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets form in clusters after petals drop. A natural drop sheds some; remaining clusters are often too crowded for good size. Petal fall is also a codling-moth timing window.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the flowers fall, little pears appear in clusters. The tree drops some on its own, but usually leaves too many close together.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to about one fruit per cluster (roughly 6 inches apart) within 4 to 6 weeks of bloom to size up fruit, reduce limb breakage, and curb biennial bearing. Target codling moth at petal fall, and watch for the first sticky signs of pear psylla.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Thin the young pears: snap off extras so you leave about one per cluster, spaced roughly a hand-width apart. Fewer pears means bigger, better fruit and less chance of a branch breaking. Petal fall is also the time to deal with the codling moth (the worm in the fruit).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record thinning date, pest treatments at petal fall, and any psylla activity.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you thinned and any pest treatment after the petals dropped.

growth_stages.name: Harvest mature-but-firm (around year 4 to 6+)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full varietal size with the green ground color lightening, corky tan lenticels, and easy detachment when lifted and twisted upward to horizontal. Pick FIRM, the flesh should still be hard. Different varieties ripen weeks apart; do not wait for softening on the tree.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Pears reach full size and the green starts to lighten, and they snap off easily when you lift and twist them up. They will still be hard, and that is right. Do not wait for them to soften on the tree.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick mature but firm as each variety comes ready (first real crop usually around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent). Cool-store to satisfy post-harvest chilling, then ripen at room temperature. Handle gently to avoid bruising.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pick the pears while firm as each kind comes ready (your first real harvest is usually around the fourth to sixth year). Put them somewhere cold for a while, then bring a few out to finish ripening on the counter. Handle them gently so they do not bruise.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates, firmness at picking, cold-storage start, and ripening results by variety.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked (while firm), and how they ripened indoors.

growth_stages.name: Post-harvest and fall sanitation
growth_stages.timing: fall, after harvest into leaf drop
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves yellow and drop as the tree re-enters dormancy. Note dropped fruit and fallen leaves (carryover sources for codling moth, scab, and Fabraea leaf spot).
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After harvest the leaves turn and fall, and the tree goes to sleep for winter. Look at what is left on the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves (breaks pear scab and Fabraea cycles) and clear dropped fruit (breaks codling moth). A late-fall or dormant horticultural oil sets up pear-psylla control. Do not prune now, wait for late-winter dormancy and dry weather.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Rake up and remove the fallen leaves and any pears on the ground, this one chore prevents a lot of next-year disease and pests. Do not prune yet, save that for late winter when it is dry.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record fall sanitation done and tree condition going into dormancy.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note that you cleaned up leaves and fruit, and how the tree looks heading into winter.

notifications.title_beginner: Pinch off the flowers this year
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in its establishment year. Remove the blossoms now so energy goes to roots and scaffold, not fruit.
notifications.body_beginner: It is your tree's first year. Pinch off any flowers that open, no pears yet. This builds a much stronger tree.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through the first summer, deep-soak 1 to 2 times per week to establish roots. Do not let the root ball dry out.
notifications.body_beginner: All this first summer, give your tree a deep soak once or twice a week so the roots get going. Do not let it dry out.

notifications.title_beginner: Late-winter oil spray for pear psylla
notifications.body_seasoned: Apply dormant horticultural oil in late winter to smother overwintering pear psylla adults and eggs before bud break, the backbone of psylla control.
notifications.body_beginner: While the tree is bare in late winter, spray horticultural oil to smother the overwintering pear psylla (a sticky-honeydew pest specific to pears) before the buds open.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time for the annual dormant prune
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now in late winter before bud break, in dry weather: thin for light and air, remove dead, crossing, and water-sprout wood, and cut out fire-blight cankers.
notifications.body_beginner: It is late winter and the tree is bare, the right time to prune, but only when it is dry out. Thin out branches so light gets in, and cut dead, crossing, or fire-blight-burned wood.

notifications.title_beginner: Frost can kill the flowers now
notifications.body_seasoned: The tree is blooming, often a few days before apples, so the bloom is more frost-exposed. A hard late frost on open blossoms can eliminate this year's crop, watch the forecast and protect small trees.
notifications.body_beginner: Your tree is flowering, a bit earlier than apples, so frost is a real risk. A hard frost right now can wipe out this year's pears. Watch the forecast and cover a small tree if frost is coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin fruit and target petal-fall pests
notifications.title_beginner: Thin pears and check for pests
notifications.body_seasoned: Within 4 to 6 weeks of bloom, thin to about one fruit per cluster. Petal fall is the codling-moth timing window; also scout for the first sticky honeydew of pear psylla.
notifications.body_beginner: Now that petals have dropped, snap off extra little pears so you leave about one per cluster. This is also the time to deal with the codling moth (the worm in the fruit).

notifications.body_seasoned: Check maturity by ground color lightening, corky lenticels, and easy upward-twist detachment, then pick FIRM and ripen off the tree. Varieties ripen weeks apart; do not let them soften on the branch.
notifications.body_beginner: Start checking your pears: full size, green lightening, and they snap off when lifted and twisted up. Pick them while still hard and ripen them indoors, never on the tree.

notifications.title_seasoned: Fall cleanup: rake leaves and clear drops
notifications.title_beginner: Rake up leaves and fallen pears
notifications.body_seasoned: After harvest, rake and remove fallen leaves (breaks pear scab and Fabraea leaf spot) and clear dropped fruit (breaks codling moth).
notifications.body_beginner: After picking, rake up the fallen leaves and any pears on the ground. This one chore prevents a lot of next-year disease and pests.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Frost coming while your tree flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard frost is forecast while the tree is in bloom. Pear blooms early and its open blossoms and young fruitlets are frost-tender, protect small trees with covers or run sprinklers through the frost.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is on the way while your pear tree is flowering. The flowers can be killed by cold, which means no pears this year. Cover a small tree, or run a sprinkler over it through the cold night.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Warm, wet weather raises a serious disease risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, wet conditions during bloom strongly favor fire blight infection through pear blossoms, which are highly susceptible. Do not prune in the wet, and follow a fire-blight forecast model if available.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm and wet while the tree is blooming is exactly when fire blight (a serious disease that pears catch easily) spreads. Do not prune in wet weather right now, and watch for blackened branch tips.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell while pears are growing
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained heat during fruit sizing increases water demand and the risk of premature fruit drop and sunscald. Keep soil moisture even with a weekly deep soak.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hot stretch while the pears are filling out means the tree needs more water. Keep watering steady so the fruit does not drop early.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: High wind can drop fruit and break fruit-laden limbs, especially on dwarf and quince-rooted trees. Check stakes and supports; harvest mature-firm fruit ahead of a major blow.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Strong wind can knock pears down and snap branches loaded with fruit. Check that your tree's stake is solid, and pick any mature firm pears before a big storm.

planting.text_seasoned: Keep the graft union 2 to 3 inches above the soil line, burying it lets the variety root and lose the rootstock's size and disease benefits.
planting.text_beginner: Keep the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the variety was joined to the roots) 2 to 3 in above the soil. If you bury it, the top variety grows its own roots and the tree loses the size control and disease resistance the rootstock gives it.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant a compatible, bloom-overlapping pollinizer at the same time, a lone pear (or an incompatible pair like Bartlett with Seckel) wastes years.
planting.text_beginner: Plant a second, different pear variety at the same time so they can pollinate each other, and check they are compatible (Bartlett and Seckel are not). A single pear, or a mismatched pair, usually makes no fruit.

establishment.text_seasoned: Pinch off every blossom the first spring, a fruitless year 1 builds a stronger tree for the decades pear lives.
establishment.text_beginner: Pinch off all the flowers the first spring. Going without fruit in year 1 lets the tree put its energy into roots and branches, which makes it much stronger for the long life ahead.

establishment.text_seasoned: Mulch a wide ring but keep it a few inches off the trunk to avoid rot and rodent cover.
establishment.text_beginner: Spread mulch in a wide circle around the tree, but keep it a few inches away from the trunk. Mulch against the trunk holds rot-causing moisture and hides mice that chew bark.

establishment.text_seasoned: Aim for about 12 to 18 inches of new shoot growth a year, much more means too much nitrogen, which on a pear directly feeds fire blight.
establishment.text_beginner: A young pear should grow about 12 to 18 in of new branch each year. A lot more than that means too much nitrogen (the leafy-growth nutrient), which on pears feeds the disease fire blight, so ease off feeding.

establishment.text_seasoned: Protect the young trunk from sunscald and voles with a light-colored guard over the first winters.
establishment.text_beginner: Protect the young trunk through its first few winters with a light-colored tree guard. This prevents sunscald (bark damage from winter sun) and stops voles from chewing the bark.

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Pears grow naturally upright and narrow, so train the framework with limb spreaders to widen crotch angles while the wood is young, and prune conservatively in dry weather, heavy cuts force the succulent regrowth fire blight exploits. The shape you set in the first few years is the shape the tree keeps for decades.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Pears want to grow tall and narrow, so in the first few winters gently push the upright branches outward with small spreaders to build a strong, open shape. Prune only a little, and only when it is dry, because hard pruning makes soft growth that catches fire blight. The shape you set now is the shape the tree keeps for life.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune in late winter before bud break and only in dry weather; pruning a pear in humid conditions opens cuts to fire blight.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Do your pruning in late winter, before the buds open, and only when the weather is dry. Cuts made in damp weather let in fire blight, a serious disease that blackens and kills pear branches.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Disinfect pruners between cuts whenever fire blight may be present, and cut cankers 8 to 12 inches below visible damage.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: If fire blight might be around, wipe your pruners with disinfectant between each cut, and when you remove a burnt-looking branch, cut well below the damage (about a hand's length past it).

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Dormancy is when the tree banks its chill hours, the cold is doing necessary work, not harm.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: In winter the leafless tree is resting and collecting its chill hours (the cold it needs in order to flower and fruit later). The cold is helping the tree, not hurting it.

bloom.text_seasoned: Never spray insecticide during bloom, and remember pear nectar is low, so you need every bee that visits.
bloom.text_beginner: Never spray bug killer while the tree is in bloom. Pear flowers do not attract many bees to begin with, and insecticide kills the few you are counting on to set fruit.

bloom.text_seasoned: Watch the frost forecast: pear blooms early, so a hard frost on open blossoms can cost the whole crop.
bloom.text_beginner: Keep an eye on the frost forecast while the tree is flowering. Pears bloom early, so a hard frost can destroy the whole year's crop, cover the tree if a freeze is coming.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin to one fruit per cluster within about a month of bloom for bigger pears and steadier yearly crops.
fruit_set.text_beginner: About a month after bloom, thin the tiny pears to one per cluster by pinching off extras. Fewer pears per cluster means bigger fruit and a more even crop year to year.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Petal fall is the codling-moth timing window; also scout the new shoots for the first sticky honeydew of pear psylla.
fruit_set.text_beginner: The time right after petals fall is the key window to control codling moth (the worm in the fruit). Also check the new shoots for sticky, shiny goo, the sign of pear psylla.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick mature but FIRM and ripen off the tree: full size, ground color lightening, lenticels corky, and the stem snapping free on an upward twist. A tree-ripened pear browns and turns gritty at the core.
harvest.text_beginner: A pear is ready to pick, not eat, when it is full-sized, the green is lightening, and it snaps off when you lift and twist it up. It will still be hard, and that is right. Ripen them indoors, a pear left to ripen on the tree rots from the inside.

harvest.text_seasoned: Give winter pears (Anjou, Bosc) a cold rest near freezing for several weeks before ripening; summer Bartlett ripens after just a few days cool.
harvest.text_beginner: Winter pears like Anjou and Bosc need a few weeks in the cold (the fridge works) before they will ripen on the counter; summer Bartlett needs only a few days of cool. Then warm them up to finish.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves, this single chore breaks the pear-scab and Fabraea-leaf-spot cycles for next year.
post_harvest.text_beginner: Rake up and remove the fallen leaves in autumn. This one chore breaks the cycle of pear scab and Fabraea leaf spot (two leaf-spotting fungi that overwinter in old leaves) for next year.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear dropped fruit to break the codling-moth cycle, and apply a dormant oil to set up pear-psylla control.
post_harvest.text_beginner: Pick up every dropped pear to break the codling-moth cycle, and a late-fall or winter spray of horticultural oil helps knock back pear psylla for next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Mature yield is rootstock-driven: a size-controlled tree (quince or OHxF 333) carries roughly 1 to 2 bushels (about 40 to 80 lb) per year, a semi-vigorous OHxF 87/97 more, and a standard seedling-rooted tree can exceed 4 to 8 bushels at full maturity. Pears tend to bear heavily once established.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: How many pears you get depends mostly on tree size. A small tree gives roughly 1 to 2 bushels a year (a bushel is about 40 lb of pears), while a full-size tree can give several times that once mature. Established pears often crop heavily.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing several years after first crop: roughly years 6 to 10, later than apple and later still on standard rootstocks. Many cultivars tend toward biennial bearing (a heavy year then a light one); consistent fruit thinning evens it out.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A pear does not hit full production right away, it builds up over several years after its first crop, a bit slower than an apple. Some varieties naturally swing between a big year and a small year; thinning the young fruit helps keep crops steadier.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No crop in the planting year (blossoms are removed). First meaningful fruit around year 4 to 6, rootstock-dependent and later than apple.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Expect zero pears the first year, that is normal and intended. Your first real handful of fruit usually comes around year 4 to 6, a bit later than an apple.
factors_seasoned: rootstock (sets tree size, bearing age, and fire-blight/decline tolerance)
cross-pollination success (compatible, overlapping pollinizer within ~50 to 100 ft)
fire blight and pear psylla pressure

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No research-backed lunar planting preference applies to pear; dormant bare-root planting timing is driven by soil workability and the dormant window, not moon phase.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree flowered but set no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of flowers, but no pears
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Without a compatible pollinizer in overlapping bloom within about 50 to 100 ft, pear blossoms are not fertilized and drop. A common trap is an INCOMPATIBLE pair (Bartlett with Seckel) or a pollen-sterile variety (Magness) used as the lone partner.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your tree had plenty of flowers but they fell off without making pears. Usually there was no second, compatible pear variety blooming nearby. Watch for two traps: Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other, and Magness cannot pollinate anything.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Add a second, genetically different, COMPATIBLE pear whose bloom overlaps, within about 50 to 100 ft (check the compatibility chart). Strong bee activity helps, since pear nectar is low.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Plant a second, different pear variety nearby that blooms at the same time and is a compatible match, then bees can do their job. Avoid the Bartlett-Seckel mismatch.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Branches turned black, as if burned
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) infected through blossoms or tender shoots in warm, wet weather, blackening shoots into shepherd's crooks and forming cankers. Pear is highly susceptible, and lush nitrogen-pushed growth made it worse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Branch tips suddenly turned black and bent into a hook, as if scorched. This is fire blight, the main pear disease, which spreads in warm, wet weather and loves the soft growth from too much fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut out infected wood 8 to 12 inches below symptoms in dry weather, disinfecting between cuts; going forward plant resistant cultivars (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow) on a tolerant rootstock and keep nitrogen lean.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cut the blackened branches well below the damage in dry weather, wiping tools between cuts. Next time choose a resistant variety, go easy on fertilizer, and only prune when it is dry.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Pears brown and gritty at the core
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The fruit was left to ripen on the tree, or held too warm too long after picking. European pears ripen from the inside out and break down at the core (stone-cell grit, internal browning) if tree-ripened or over-held.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: You cut open a pear and the middle was brown and gritty while the outside looked fine. That happens when pears ripen on the tree instead of being picked firm and ripened indoors.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pick mature but FIRM (upward-twist detachment, lightening ground color), cool-store to satisfy post-harvest chilling, then ripen at room temperature and eat promptly once the neck softens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Next time pick the pears while still firm and green, give them a cold rest, then ripen them on the counter and eat them soon after they soften.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Few flowers, or flowers very late
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A high-chill variety grown in a warm-winter zone did not accumulate enough chill to break dormancy normally, giving delayed, uneven, weak bloom and poor set. European pears need more chill than apples, so the mismatch is easy to make.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The tree barely flowered, or flowered oddly late and patchy. This usually means the variety needs more winter cold than your area gives, and pears need more cold than apples.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match variety chill to your winters: in warm zones choose low-chill cultivars (Hood, Kieffer, Orient).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick a low-chill pear variety suited to mild winters, like Hood, Kieffer, or Orient. The right variety for your climate flowers normally.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Sticky leaves with black sooty mold
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pear psylla nymphs fed heavily and exuded honeydew that grew black sooty mold, scorching leaves and russeting fruit. Outbreaks often follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill the psylla's natural enemies.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The leaves and young pears got coated in sticky goo that turned black and grimy. That is pear psylla, a pear-specific insect; it gets worse if harsh sprays have killed the helpful bugs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Apply dormant oil in late winter, use insecticidal soap or summer oil in season, and conserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Spray dormant oil in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, use insecticidal soap during the season, and avoid harsh sprays that kill the good bugs.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Heavy crop one year, almost none the next
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: A huge year, then a bare year
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The tree fell into biennial bearing: a heavy crop suppressed next year's flower buds, giving an off year. Some pear varieties are naturally prone to it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: One year the tree was loaded, the next it had almost none. Pears can get into this on-and-off rhythm when they over-crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin fruit consistently every year (about one per cluster) so the tree sets flower buds for the following season and crops more evenly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Thin the young pears every single year, even in a big year. Leaving fewer pears helps the tree make flower buds for next year and evens out the crops.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Not applicable. Succession planting (re-sowing in waves for a continuous harvest) is an annual-vegetable practice. Pear is a perennial tree that holds its site for decades and bears once a year, so there is no succession to schedule; continuity comes from variety choice (summer through winter pears) and storage, not replanting.
